DOCUMENT:
Internal Audit Memo: Missed Appointments in Outpatient Physiotherapy
To: Director of Operations, Therapies Division
From: Clinical Audit Team
Date: 14 August 2026

1. Scope
This audit examined missed appointments in the outpatient physiotherapy service across our three clinic sites between 1 January and 30 June 2026. For the purposes of this audit, a "did not attend" (DNA) is recorded when a patient fails to attend without giving notice. Late cancellations (less than 24 hours' notice) are recorded and reported separately, because the slot can sometimes be offered to another patient. We reviewed the appointment system records for all 24,860 booked appointments in the period and interviewed reception and clinical staff at each site.

2. Overall position
There were 2,610 DNAs in the period, a DNA rate of 10.5%, against the service target of 8%. Each DNA leaves a 30-minute clinical slot unused. At the service's average cost per clinical hour of £62, the 1,305 lost clinical hours represent around £80,900 of clinical time over six months.

Table 1. DNA rate by appointment type
Appointment type | Booked | DNAs | DNA rate
New patient assessment | 6,210 | 410 | 6.6%
Follow-up | 18,650 | 2,200 | 11.8%
Total | 24,860 | 2,610 | 10.5%

Follow-up appointments account for most DNAs. Staff told us that many patients stop attending once their symptoms improve, without telling the service.

3. Reminder calls
Since 2024, reception staff have phoned patients two working days before their appointment where time allows. In the audit period, staff made reminder calls for 7,800 appointments, about 300 a week over the 26 weeks. A call is recorded as received only if the patient answered and confirmed they would attend; unanswered calls are not recorded. Reception staff estimate that each call, including dialling, rescheduling where needed and updating the record, takes an average of four minutes.

Table 2. DNA rate by reminder status
Reminder status | Appointments | DNAs | DNA rate
Reminder call received | 7,800 | 470 | 6.0%
No reminder call recorded | 17,060 | 2,140 | 12.5%

Patients who received a reminder call were less than half as likely to miss their appointment. Reminder calls therefore more than halve the DNA rate, and extending them to all appointments would bring the service well within its 8% target.

4. Discharge policy
The service's policy is that a patient who DNAs twice without explanation is discharged back to their referrer. We found the policy was applied inconsistently: of 160 patients who met the criterion, 104 were discharged. Staff were reluctant to discharge patients they knew to be vulnerable.

5. Late cancellations
In addition to the DNAs above, 1,140 appointments were cancelled with less than 24 hours' notice. Reception staff were able to refill 31% of these slots, usually with patients on the cancellation list.

6. Findings and recommendations
Finding 1. The DNA rate of 10.5% (including late cancellations, which we classify as DNAs) is above target and costs the service around £80,900 in clinical time every six months.
Recommendation 1. Extend reminder calls to all booked appointments, about 960 a week, using reception staff. This can be absorbed within existing reception hours at no additional cost.

Finding 2. The two-DNA discharge policy is applied inconsistently.
Recommendation 2. Revise the policy to include a documented clinical review before discharge, so that vulnerable patients are protected and the policy can then be applied consistently.

Finding 3. Late-cancellation slots are refilled only 31% of the time.
Recommendation 3. Introduce an automated text offer to patients on the cancellation list when a slot becomes free.

7. Conclusion
Missed appointments are costly but largely preventable. Reminder calls have been shown to more than halve DNAs in this service, and extending them to every patient, together with the policy and process changes above, should bring the DNA rate below target within six months.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "The DNA rate of 10.5% (including late cancellations, which we classify as DNAs)" -- Section 1 defines DNAs as failures to attend without notice and says late cancellations are recorded and reported separately (and section 5 reports 1,140 late cancellations 'in addition to the DNAs above'). Finding 1 says the 10.5% includes late cancellations classified as DNAs. The definition contradicts itself.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "Reminder calls therefore more than halve the DNA rate" -- A call is only recorded as 'received' if the patient answered and confirmed attendance; unanswered calls fall into the comparison group. The groups are selected on engagement/intention to attend, and calls were made only 'where time allows', so the 6.0% vs 12.5% difference does not show the calls caused the reduction.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "This can be absorbed within existing reception hours at no additional cost." -- The document states each call takes about four minutes and staff currently make about 300 calls a week. Going to about 960 a week adds about 660 calls, roughly 44 extra staff hours a week (more than one full-time post). The memo never addresses this workload/cost although its own data raise it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Internal Audit Memo on Missed Appointments in Outpatient Physiotherapy

## Summary

The descriptive figures are internally consistent. I checked the arithmetic:

- 2,610 / 24,860 = 10.5%
- 1,305 hours × £62 ≈ £80,900
- Table 1 and Table 2 both sum correctly to 24,860 appointments and 2,610 DNAs.

However, the memo's central claim does not follow from its data. That claim is that reminder calls "more than halve" DNAs and that extending them would bring the service within target. The main recommendation is also costed in a way the memo's own figures contradict. There is also a definitional contradiction in the findings. These need fixing before the memo goes to the Director.

## Major issues

### 1. The reminder-call comparison cannot support a causal claim

Section 3 defines "received" as a call where the patient **answered and confirmed they would attend**. Unanswered calls are not recorded, so those patients fall into the "no reminder call recorded" group. This creates severe selection bias:

- **The comparison is circular.** The "received" group consists of patients who had just told staff they would attend. A lower DNA rate there partly reflects that stated intention, not the effect of the call.
- **The comparison group is contaminated.** It includes patients who were called but didn't answer. That group is plausibly the least engaged and most likely to DNA, which inflates the 12.5%.
- **Calls are not allocated at random.** They are made "where time allows", and the memo doesn't say how patients are chosen. If calls fall unevenly by appointment type, site, or patient characteristics, the comparison is confounded. For example, new patients have a lower baseline DNA rate (6.6% vs 11.8%), so calling more of them would flatter the results. The memo should at least break Table 2 down by appointment type and site.

The statement that reminders "have been shown to more than halve DNAs in this service" is therefore unsupported. Auditing every appointment makes the rates exact, but it does nothing to remove this bias. The true effect of extending calls could be much smaller than 6.5 percentage points. The 8% target could still be missed.

**Better evidence options:**

- Record every call attempt and its outcome, and compare by intention-to-call.
- Use the 2024 introduction of calls for a before/after comparison.
- Pilot the extension at one site against the other two.

### 2. The "no additional cost" claim contradicts the memo's own figures

- **Current effort is understated.** About 300 confirmed calls a week × 4 minutes = about 20 staff-hours a week. That counts only answered calls. Unanswered attempts also take time and are not recorded, so the real current effort is higher.
- **The proposed workload is large.** About 960 calls a week × 4 minutes = **about 64 hours a week**, roughly 1.7 FTE. That is an extra 44+ hours a week before counting unanswered attempts and redials.
- **The memo implies there is no spare capacity.** Calls are currently made only "where time allows". That suggests reception does not have spare capacity now, let alone 44+ more hours a week.

The memo should either cost this properly or explain where the time comes from. The author's statement that the plan "does not need new funding" is not supported. Recommendation 3, an automated text system, is also likely to have procurement or licensing costs.

### 3. Finding 1 contradicts the stated DNA definition

Section 1 says late cancellations are recorded and reported separately. Finding 1 says the 10.5% rate is "including late cancellations, which we classify as DNAs".

The 10.5% figure clearly excludes them. Including the 1,140 late cancellations would give 3,750 / 24,860 = **15.1%**. This sentence must be corrected, since it undermines the definitional care the memo otherwise shows.

## Moderate issues

### 4. The £80,900 is not a cash saving

Clinicians are still paid during DNA slots, and some of that time is likely used for notes or admin. The figure is best described as the opportunity cost or lost capacity, for example 1,305 hours, or about 2,610 appointments that could have treated waiting-list patients. Presenting it as money "at stake" risks it being read as recoverable savings.

The cost of unfilled late cancellations is also omitted: about 787 slots, or about 393 hours, and roughly £24,400 on the same basis.

### 5. The target projection is unsupported

"Well within its 8% target" and "below target within six months" both assume that every patient reached by an extended service would behave like today's self-selected confirmers. Many extra calls will go unanswered. Some patients will cancel in response rather than attend. That is still useful, since the slot can be refilled, but it is not the same as attending.

### 6. The main driver identified is not addressed

The memo identifies follow-up patients who stop attending once their symptoms improve as the largest source of DNAs. No recommendation targets this directly. Options worth considering include:

- patient-initiated follow-up
- asking at each visit whether a further appointment is needed
- making it easy to cancel by text

### 7. The discharge policy finding is thin

- The 104 of 160 (65%) compliance figure has no context. We don't know how many of the 56 non-discharges were justified by vulnerability.
- Adding a clinical review is sensible for safety, but it will likely reduce discharges. It may make the policy more consistent, but it is not clear it reduces DNAs.
- The memo doesn't state the expected impact of this recommendation.

## Minor points

- The 31% refill rate needs a benchmark or an explanation of why slots weren't filled, such as short notice or an empty cancellation list. Without that, it's unclear whether automated texts address the actual bottleneck.
- Results aren't broken down by site, despite the audit covering three sites and interviewing staff at each.
- Calling the reminder call "low-tech" is fair, but "low-cost" is not established (see issue 2).

## Suggested revisions

1. Reframe Section 3 as an observed association with known bias, not proof of effect. Recommend a properly recorded pilot before full rollout.
2. Cost the reminder extension in staff-hours or FTE, including unanswered attempts. Remove "no additional cost" unless capacity is demonstrated.
3. Correct Finding 1's late-cancellation statement. Optionally report a combined "lost slot" rate (15.1%) alongside it.
4. Describe £80,900 as lost clinical capacity rather than savings.
5. Add a recommendation that targets follow-up drop-off directly.
6. Soften the conclusion's six-month target projection.
